title: Why women get tailbone pain five times more often than men
summary: Women are about five times more likely than men to develop coccydynia. Pelvis shape, childbirth and pregnancy hormones all play a part. Here is what the research shows.
text: One of the most consistent findings about coccydynia is that it affects women far more often than men: about five women for every man . The reasons are a mix of anatomy, pregnancy and childbirth. Key points - Women are about 5 times more likely than men to develop coccydynia. - A woman's pelvis is wider and differently angled , so the coccyx is more exposed when sitting. - Childbirth can push the coccyx backward. In one specialist clinic it accounted for 7.3% of women's coccydynia cases, and forceps had been used in about half of those deliveries. - Pelvic girdle pain affects about 1 in 5 pregnant women and can overlap with tailbone pain. - Pain after childbirth is often dismissed as "normal". If it lasts beyond a few weeks, it deserves an assessment. Reason 1: the shape of the pelvis A woman's pelvis is wider and shallower, which is needed for childbirth. When she sits, the coccyx sits further back relative to the sitting bones and is more likely to share the load. Reviews also point to greater ligament laxity and differences in coccyx shape. In men, the narrower pelvis tends to keep the coccyx clear of the seat. Reason 2: childbirth During a vaginal delivery, the baby's head pushes the coccyx backward. Usually it springs back, but a difficult or assisted delivery can strain the ligaments or push a joint out of place. Finding in 57 women with coccydynia after childbirth Result Share of all women's coccydynia cases in the clinic linked to childbirth 7.3% Forceps used at delivery 50.8% Vacuum-assisted delivery 7.0% Spontaneous but "difficult" delivery 12.3% Coccyx joint slipped (luxation) 43.9% (vs 17.0% in women with coccydynia from other causes) Coccyx fracture 5.3% Linked to more luxation BMI above 27, and two or more vaginal deliveries Postpartum coccydynia (Maigne et al., 2012). Reason 3: pregnancy and pelvic girdle pain During pregnancy, hormones loosen the ligaments of the pelvis. Pelvic girdle pain (pain at the back of the pelvis or over the pubic bone) affects about 20% of pregnant women at any one time. It is a separate condition, but it can sit alongside tailbone pain and makes sitting and walking harder. A Norwegian study of a multi-ethnic group of women found that women of South Asian and Middle Eastern origin reported 10–20% more pelvic girdle pain than Western women at every stage of pregnancy and after birth. The difference was not significant once other factors were taken into account, so it may reflect circumstances such as the number of children rather than ethnicity itself. Why diagnosis is often late Many women assume tailbone pain after delivery is part of recovery, or feel embarrassed to mention it. But pain that stops you sitting to feed your baby, or that is still there after a few weeks, is worth having examined. Hands-on treatment for a displaced or stiff coccyx is gentle and usually needs only a few visits. A female clinician is available at our clinic if you prefer.

title: Two-wheelers, potholes and tailbone pain: what the research shows
summary: A 2025 study found tailbone pain in a third of regular motorbike riders, and vibration was the strongest risk factor. What that means for daily commuters in Delhi, and how to protect your coccyx.
text: For millions of people in Indian cities, the daily commute means a scooter or motorbike: speed breakers, potholes and long rides in traffic. Each bump travels up through a narrow seat to the base of your spine. Research from our region suggests that this matters for the tailbone. Key points - A 2025 study of 190 male riders in Pakistan found tailbone pain in 33.2% . - Vibration exposure was the strongest risk factor: riders exposed to it were almost 6 times more likely to have pain. - Poor posture on the bike roughly tripled the odds. - Riders with weak core muscles (unable to hold a plank) all reported pain. - Long sitting hours alone, bike type and bike fit were not significantly linked to pain in this study. What the study found Factor Finding Strength of link Overall tailbone pain 33.2% of 190 riders — Exposure to vibration 70% of exposed riders had pain Odds ratio 5.79 (strong) Poor riding posture 51.2% had pain Odds ratio 2.71 Unable to hold a plank 100% had pain Small group; suggests core strength matters Bike type, bike fit, occupation, sitting hours No significant link — Coccydynia among male bike riders aged 16–40 (Fatima et al., 2025). About the evidence: this is one cross-sectional study of young men in Pakistan. It shows an association, not proof that riding causes coccydynia. We have not found a similar study in India yet, but road conditions and commuting habits are very similar. Why vibration is hard on the coccyx The coccyx is a small bone with several joints, held by ligaments and the pelvic-floor muscles. A single hard bump can bruise it. Thousands of smaller jolts every week may strain the ligaments and keep the area irritated, especially if you are already sitting at a desk for hours. The MSD Manual lists motorcycling and cycling among the activities that patients with coccydynia are advised to limit while they recover. Protecting your tailbone on two wheels 1. Slow down for speed breakers and potholes , and lift slightly off the seat for big bumps. 2. Sit upright, slightly forward , with your weight on your sitting bones rather than slouched back. 3. Check your seat: add a firm, shock-absorbing seat cover, and keep your tyres at the right pressure. 4. Strengthen your core: simple plank and bridge exercises support the pelvis. 5. Break up long rides , and combine this with regular breaks if you also sit all day. 6. If it already hurts , take a break from riding, or ride pillion with a cut-out cushion, until you have been assessed.

title: When it isn't the coccyx: conditions that can mimic tailbone pain
summary: Pilonidal cysts, nerve pain, cysts on the sacral nerves, stress fractures and, rarely, tumours can all feel like tailbone pain. How they differ, and why a careful examination comes first.
text: Most pain at the base of the spine really does come from the coccyx and the muscles around it. But a few other conditions can feel very similar, and some need quite different treatment. This is why every patient is examined carefully before treatment starts. Key points - Pilonidal cysts sit in the skin over the tailbone, not in the bone. They often cause a tender lump, redness or discharge. - Pudendal nerve pain is burning or shooting pain in the genitals, perineum or back passage, typically worse sitting and better standing or on a toilet seat. - Tarlov cysts on the sacral nerves are usually harmless and found by chance, but large ones occasionally cause pain. - Sacral insufficiency fractures happen without a fall in people with weak bones, mostly older women. - Tumours near the sacrum and coccyx, such as chordoma, are rare. Constant pain, pain at night and weight loss are warning signs. How they compare Condition Where it comes from Clues that point to it Coccydynia The coccyx joints, ligaments and attached muscles Pain you can point to with one finger, worse when sitting and when getting up from sitting; tender coccyx on examination Pilonidal cyst or abscess Skin and hair follicles in the cleft between the buttocks A lump, redness, warmth, a small pit or discharge in the skin; the bone itself isn't tender Pudendal neuralgia The pudendal nerve Burning, stabbing or numb pain in the genitals, perineum or anus; worse sitting, eased by standing, lying or sitting on a toilet seat Tarlov (perineural) cyst Fluid-filled sacs on the sacral nerve roots Often no symptoms; sometimes sacral pain, buttock or leg pain, or bladder and bowel changes; seen on MRI Sacral insufficiency fracture A stress fracture of the sacrum in weakened bone Older age, osteoporosis, steroids or past pelvic radiotherapy; sudden low back or buttock pain without a fall Endometriosis Tissue like the womb lining growing in the pelvis Pain that follows the menstrual cycle, painful periods or intercourse Chordoma and other tumours The bone of the sacrum or coccyx, or tissue in front of it Constant pain, pain at night or at rest, weight loss, a growing lump, bladder or bowel problems Infection or bowel disease Bone infection (osteomyelitis), rectal disease Fever, feeling unwell, bleeding from the back passage, change in bowel habit Conditions that can feel like tailbone pain, and how they usually differ (MSD Manual; Cleveland Clinic; Radiopaedia). Pilonidal cysts A pilonidal cyst forms when hair and skin debris get trapped under the skin in the cleft between the buttocks. It is a skin problem, not a bone problem, and is treated by a surgeon or dermatologist. It is more common in young adults and people who sit for long periods. If you see or feel a lump, redness or discharge, have it checked. Pudendal neuralgia The pudendal nerve supplies the genitals, the perineum (the area between the legs) and the anus. When it is irritated or compressed, it causes nerve-type pain (burning, electric, pins and needles or numbness) in those areas. Like coccydynia it is worse when sitting, but the pain is felt more at the front and in the middle of the pelvis than at the tailbone itself. Cycling, long sitting and childbirth are known triggers. Tarlov cysts These small sacs of spinal fluid on the nerve roots of the sacrum are common on MRI scans and usually cause no symptoms at all. Finding one doesn't mean it is causing your pain. Only occasionally, when a cyst is large and its symptoms match, is it thought to be the cause. Sacral insufficiency fractures In people with weak bones, the sacrum can crack under normal body weight, with no fall. It is easy to miss on plain X-rays; MRI or CT shows it. Anyone over about 60, especially women with osteoporosis, who develops sudden pain low in the back or buttocks should have this considered. Endometriosis In endometriosis, tissue like the lining of the womb grows elsewhere in the pelvis. Deep endometriosis behind the womb can occasionally cause pain felt low in the back or near the tailbone. The key clue is that the pain follows the menstrual cycle. This needs a gynaecologist's assessment. Tumours: rare, but important Growths in or in front of the sacrum and coccyx, such as chordoma, sacrococcygeal teratoma or a tailgut cyst, are rare. They are mentioned here because they can be missed if tailbone pain is never examined. The warning signs are listed in our article on red flags in tailbone pain. Why examination comes first Coccydynia has a typical pattern, and a careful history and hands-on examination usually confirm it. When the story or the examination doesn't fit, or a red flag is present, we refer you for the right test or specialist before any treatment. Scans are requested only when they will change what we do.

title: A short history of tailbone pain: from 1859 to today
summary: Tailbone pain was named "coccygodynia" in 1859. How doctors' understanding grew, from pelvic floor spasm to coccyx shapes and sitting X-rays, and what it means for treatment today.
text: Tailbone pain is not a new problem. It has been described for centuries, and named for more than 160 years. Knowing how ideas about it developed explains why treatment today looks at the bone, the joints and the muscles. Key points - Accounts of pain at the tailbone go back to the 16th century . - In 1859 , the Scottish obstetrician Sir James Young Simpson named it coccygodynia , from the Greek for coccyx and pain. - In 1950 and 1963 , George Thiele linked many cases to spasm of the pelvic floor muscles, and treated them with massage of those muscles. - In 1983 , Postacchini and Massobrio described the different shapes of the coccyx. - In 2000 , Maigne and colleagues used X-rays taken sitting and standing to show how the coccyx moves, and linked body weight to the type of problem. - In 2014 , a study found tailbone pain about three times more often in people with ankylosing spondylitis than in people with ordinary back pain. Milestones Year Who What changed 1500s Early medical writers First written accounts of pain at the tailbone 1859 Sir James Young Simpson Named the condition coccygodynia 1950, 1963 George H. Thiele Linked tailbone pain to pelvic floor muscle spasm; treated it with massage of those muscles from inside the back passage 1983 F. Postacchini and M. Massobrio Described four coccyx shapes from X-rays (later extended to six) 1991 C. C. Wray and colleagues Compared manipulation, injections and surgery in 120 patients 2000 J. Y. Maigne and colleagues Sitting and standing X-rays showed an unstable coccyx in many patients; linked higher body weight to the coccyx slipping backwards 2014 R. Deniz and colleagues Reported tailbone pain in 38% of people with ankylosing spondylitis Milestones in understanding coccydynia. What it means today Each step added a piece of the picture: - The muscles matter. Thiele's work is why hands-on treatment of the pelvic floor is still part of care today. - The shape and movement of the coccyx matter. Postacchini and Maigne showed that the coccyx's shape and how it moves when you sit help explain the pain and guide treatment. Read more in coccyx shapes and movement. - Other conditions can be involved. Newer research links tailbone pain with inflammatory spine disease, pelvic floor problems and more. See conditions linked to tailbone pain. That is why our treatment combines a careful history and examination, hands-on treatment of both the coccyx and the muscles, and advice on sitting. See coccydynia treatment, step by step.

title: Conditions linked to tailbone pain: spondylitis, pelvic floor problems and more
summary: Tailbone pain is more common in people with ankylosing spondylitis, pelvic floor dysfunction, back problems and fibromyalgia. What the studies show, and why it changes treatment.
text: Tailbone pain doesn't always start with a fall or a hard chair. Some people who live with other conditions are more likely to develop it, and knowing about these links helps get the right treatment. Key points - Ankylosing spondylitis (AS): in one study, 38.3% of people with AS had tailbone pain, about three times the rate in people with ordinary back pain. - Pelvic floor problems: half of women seeking physiotherapy for pelvic pain also had coccydynia, and nearly 8 in 10 of them had a tight coccygeus muscle. - Fibromyalgia was about five times more common in women with coccydynia in the same study. - Low back problems often occur alongside tailbone pain, so both areas should be examined. - Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis can affect the joints of the coccyx, which in some people have a true joint lining. Ankylosing spondylitis and axial spondyloarthritis Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory disease that mainly affects the spine and the sacroiliac joints. Its typical pain is worse in the morning or after rest and eases with movement. Study People studied Tailbone pain Comparison Deniz et al., 2014 (Turkey) 107 people with AS; 74 with mechanical back pain 38.3% of AS patients Women 40.9% vs 18.4%; men 36.5% vs 8.0% in the back-pain group Terlemez et al., 2022 (Turkey) 42 people with axial spondyloarthritis 13 of 42 (about 3 in 10) Linked to worse function; the authors thought reduced coccyx movement was more likely than inflammation at the ligament attachments Tailbone pain in inflammatory spine disease. Why it matters: if tailbone pain started without an injury, is worse in the morning, and comes with back stiffness, it is worth checking for inflammatory disease. That needs a rheumatologist's treatment as well as local care. Pelvic floor dysfunction The coccyx anchors several pelvic floor muscles. When these muscles stay tight or spasm, they pull on the coccyx, and a painful coccyx in turn makes them guard more. This "pain–spasm–pain" cycle is common. Finding With coccydynia (63 women) Without coccydynia (64 women) Coccygeus muscle spasm 77.8% 17.2% Stiff sacrococcygeal joint 65.1% 14.1% Pain at the anococcygeal ligament 63.5% 9.4% Poor pelvic floor coordination 77.8% 57.8% Outlet-type constipation 31.7% 10.0% Fibromyalgia 15.9% 3.1% Women seeking physiotherapy for pelvic pain (Neville et al., 2022; 127 women). Why it matters: treating only the bone, or only the muscles, often isn't enough. Hands-on treatment that releases the pelvic floor muscles and restores how the coccyx moves addresses both sides of the cycle. Low back and sacroiliac problems Pain from the lower spine or the sacroiliac joints can spread to the area around the tailbone. People with coccydynia often have back problems too. A careful examination separates pain that truly starts at the coccyx (you can usually point to it with one finger) from pain referred from higher up. Fibromyalgia and a sensitised nervous system In fibromyalgia and related conditions, the nervous system amplifies pain signals. Normal sitting pressure can then feel very painful even when the coccyx itself is not badly damaged. The MSD Manual notes that coccydynia is occasionally part of such a generalised pain condition. Treatment then works best when it combines gentle local care with sleep, activity and pain-management support. Inflammatory arthritis In some people, the joint between the sacrum and coccyx, or between the first two coccyx segments, has a true joint lining. Diseases that inflame joint linings, such as rheumatoid arthritis, can therefore reach the coccyx. The MSD Manual lists arthropathies among the less common, non-injury causes of coccyx pain.

title: The shape and movement of your tailbone: why some hurt and others don't
summary: Coccyges come in different shapes and move differently when you sit. Here is what the four classic coccyx types mean, and how too much or too little movement causes pain.
text: Your coccyx is not a fixed, useless stub. It is made of three to five small bones, usually partly fused, and it moves a little every time you sit down. Its shape and how it moves under your weight explain a large part of why some people develop tailbone pain. Key points - In 1983, Postacchini and Massobrio described four coccyx shapes . The shapes that curve or angle further forward, and a slipped joint, are more common in people with tailbone pain. - When you sit, a healthy coccyx bends forward by about 5–25° . - Too much bending (over 25°) , almost no movement (under 5°) , or a slipped joint are each linked to pain. - A small bony spur at the tip is found in about 14% of patients and can press painfully into the skin when you sit. The four coccyx shapes Type What it looks like from the side What it means Type I Gentle forward curve, tip pointing down The most common shape: about two-thirds of people without pain have it, but fewer than a third of people with unexplained coccyx pain Type II Stronger curve, tip pointing straight forward More common in people with pain Type III Sharp forward angle part-way down More common in people with pain Type IV One of the joints has slipped (subluxation) The most clearly abnormal; strongly linked to pain Coccyx shapes (Postacchini and Massobrio, 1983). Having a type II or III coccyx does not mean you will get pain. Many people with these shapes never do. Shape is one factor among several, alongside injury, body weight and how you sit. How the coccyx moves when you sit Doctors compare two side-on X-rays, one taken standing and one taken sitting. This approach was developed by the French physician Jean-Yves Maigne. Comparing the two pictures shows how much the coccyx bends or slips under your weight. Finding on sitting vs standing X-ray Movement What it suggests Normal Bends forward 5–25° Pain more likely comes from muscles, ligaments or nerves Hypermobile Bends forward more than 25° Lax, overstretched ligaments; seen more in people with a low BMI Immobile (hypomobile) Moves less than 5° Stiff or fused joints; pain is often from pressure on the tip Luxation (slipped joint) The lower part slips backward (or, less often, forward) when sitting The joint gives way under load; linked to higher BMI and recent injury Coccyx movement categories (after Maigne; summarised by Garg and Ahuja, 2021). In Maigne's study of 208 patients, this method found the likely cause of pain in about 69% of cases. A recent injury, within about a month before the pain started, made instability more likely. Why we start with your history and examination Imaging has its place, but most of the information comes from listening and a careful examination. That means finding exactly where it hurts, which movements set it off, and how the coccyx and the surrounding muscles respond to gentle pressure. Imaging is usually only needed if the pain is severe, lasts for weeks, follows a significant injury, or doesn't behave as expected.

title: Coccydynia treatment, step by step: what works and how often
summary: Tailbone pain is treated in steps, from better sitting and hands-on care to injections and, rarely, surgery. What each step involves and the success rates reported in research.
text: Most people with tailbone pain get better without surgery. Treatment works like a ladder: start with the simplest, safest steps, and climb only if they don't help enough. Reviews put the success rate of the non-surgical steps at about 9 in 10 . Key points - About 90% of people with coccydynia improve with non-surgical care. - The first step is changing how and how long you sit : a wedge or cut-out cushion, leaning forward, and regular breaks. - Manipulation of the coccyx, usually combined with an injection, helped about 75–92% of patients in older clinical series. General physiotherapy (heat, ultrasound) helped little in the same studies, so the type of hands-on treatment matters. - Injections are an option when pain persists; reported relief varies widely between studies. - Surgery (coccygectomy) is kept for a small, carefully selected group, and has a real risk of wound infection. The steps at a glance Step What it involves What studies report 1. Sitting changes Wedge or U-shaped (cut-out) cushion, leaning forward, breaks every 20–30 minutes Recommended first-line in all reviews; a cut-out or wedge cushion is preferred over a doughnut ring (MSD Manual) 2. Hands-on treatment Internal or external manipulation of the coccyx, release of the pelvic floor muscles, stretching and exercises Manipulation with injection cured about 85% in a 120-patient trial (Wray 1991); other series report 75–92% improvement (Perkins, Ramsey, summarised by Garg and Ahuja). The same trial found general physiotherapy of little help 3. Medicines Short courses of anti-inflammatory pain relief, sometimes medicines for nerve pain Helpful for symptoms; not a cure on their own 4. Injections Local anaesthetic and steroid around the coccyx, or a ganglion impar block About 60% responded to steroid and anaesthetic injections (Wray 1991); ganglion impar block helped 6 of 8 patients at 6 months in a small CT-guided study (Datir 2010) 5. Ablation Radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or the ganglion impar Used for pain that keeps coming back after injections; evidence is from small studies 6. Surgery Removal of part or all of the coccyx (coccygectomy) Needed by almost 20% in Wray's trial, with over 90% success; 85–100% improvement in carefully selected patients across studies; complication rates of 0–50% across studies, mostly wound infection Coccydynia treatment options and reported results (Garg and Ahuja 2021, unless stated). These figures come from different studies with different patients and definitions of success, so they can't be compared directly. They do show a clear pattern: the simple steps help most people, and the risky steps are only for a few. Step 1: sitting differently Sitting puts weight on the coccyx, especially when you lean back. Small changes take that pressure off: - Lean forward slightly so your weight rests on your thigh bones and sitting bones, not on the tailbone. - Use a wedge or cut-out cushion with the gap at the back. A doughnut ring can still press on the coccyx. - Stand up every 20–30 minutes , and avoid low, soft sofas. See sitting with tailbone pain for more detail. Step 2: hands-on treatment This is the core of what we do at the clinic. After a careful examination, the clinician gently moves the coccyx back towards its normal position and range of movement, and releases the tight pelvic floor muscles that pull on it (see conditions linked to tailbone pain). Treatment is usually done from the inside, through the back passage, because that is the only way to reach the front of the coccyx and the muscles attached to it. It is explained fully before it starts, and you can stop at any time. People whose coccyx is too mobile or slightly displaced when they sit often respond well. Those whose coccyx is very stiff may need more sessions or another step. This is one reason we assess the coccyx shape and movement first. Step 3: medicines Anti-inflammatory tablets or gels can ease pain while other treatment takes effect. They are not a long-term answer, and should be taken only as advised by your doctor. Step 4: injections If pain persists for several weeks despite the steps above, an injection of local anaesthetic and steroid around the painful joint can calm it down. Another option is a ganglion impar block , an injection at a small nerve cluster in front of the coccyx. Injections should be done by a specialist under X-ray or CT guidance. Steps 5 and 6: ablation and surgery For the few people whose pain continues despite everything else, radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or removal of the coccyx may be considered. Surgery gives good results in carefully chosen patients, usually those with an unstable or clearly abnormal coccyx on sitting and standing X-rays. Because the wound is close to the back passage, infection is the main risk. Our approach We start at the bottom of the ladder, with a thorough history and examination, sitting advice and hands-on treatment, and refer on only when it is genuinely needed. Most of our patients need only a few sessions. Book a consultation in Delhi or online.

title: Coccydynia in numbers: what the research really says
summary: How common is tailbone pain, who gets it, what causes it and how often treatment works: the key figures from medical research, each with its source.
text: Coccydynia (tailbone or coccyx pain) is one of the most under-studied causes of back pain. This page brings together the numbers that are actually backed by published research, explains what they mean, and is honest about what is still unknown. Key points - Nobody knows exactly how many people have coccydynia. It is thought to make up only around 1% of people seen for spine pain, but it is often missed or recorded as "low back pain". - Women are affected about five times as often as men. - Half or more of patients remember an injury such as a fall. Childbirth accounts for a smaller but important share in women. - Body weight matters at both ends: both a high and a very low body mass index (BMI) raise the risk. - About 9 in 10 people improve without surgery. The key figures at a glance Question What research reports Source How common is it? Exact incidence has not been reported; roughly 1% of people seen for musculoskeletal or spine pain Lirette 2014; BMJ Best Practice Women vs men About 5 women for every man Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Who gets it Mostly adults and teenagers; uncommon in young children Lirette 2014 Remember an injury first 50–65% of patients Garg and Ahuja 2021 Linked to childbirth 7.3% of women's cases in one specialist clinic Maigne 2012 Abnormal coccyx movement when sitting About 69% of patients on sitting and standing X-rays Maigne 2000; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Bony spur at the tip About 14% of patients Garg and Ahuja 2021 Weight above which risk rises BMI over 27.4 in women, over 29.4 in men Garg and Ahuja 2021 Better without surgery About 90% Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Coccydynia key figures. Full references are listed at the end of this article. Why the exact numbers are uncertain Coccydynia rarely gets its own diagnosis code. In many records it is grouped with general low back pain, and many people never see a doctor about it, often out of embarrassment. That is why the reviews we rely on say plainly that its true incidence is unknown. Be wary of any website quoting a precise share of the population: we could not find a reliable source for such figures. Who is more likely to get it? - Women , partly because of the shape of the pelvis and because of childbirth. See why women get tailbone pain more often. - People with a higher BMI, or who are very thin. See body weight and tailbone pain. - People who sit for long hours or ride over rough roads. See two-wheelers and tailbone pain. - People with some other conditions , such as ankylosing spondylitis or pelvic floor problems. See conditions linked to tailbone pain. High rates in particular groups Some studies have looked at specific groups of people. Their figures are much higher than the general rate, because these groups are exposed to particular risks. They should not be read as rates for a whole country. Group studied Share with tailbone pain Where and when Source People with ankylosing spondylitis 38.3% (vs 18.4% of women and 8% of men with ordinary back pain) Istanbul, Turkey, 2014; 107 patients Deniz 2014 Women seeking physiotherapy for pelvic pain 49.6% USA, 2022; 127 women Neville 2022 Male motorbike riders 33.2% Pakistan, 2025; 190 riders Fatima 2025 Long-term wheelchair users 76% South Punjab, Pakistan, 2024; 250 users Sanobar 2024 Tailbone pain in specific study groups. We have not found a published study measuring coccydynia across the general population of India. The two Pakistani studies are the closest regional data, and their settings (long sitting, motorbike commuting) are very familiar in Indian cities. How well does treatment work? Most people get better with simple measures: a cut-out cushion, changes to how and how long they sit, and hands-on treatment of the coccyx and pelvic floor muscles. Injections are an option if pain persists, and surgery is kept for a small, carefully selected group. See coccydynia treatment, step by step.

title: Body weight and tailbone pain: why both high and low BMI matter
summary: Being overweight raises the risk of coccydynia, but so does being very thin. The reason is the way your pelvis tilts when you sit. Here is the research, explained simply.
text: Body weight is one of the clearest risk factors for tailbone pain, but not in the way most people expect. Research shows that both a higher body mass index (BMI) and being very thin can lead to coccydynia, through two different mechanisms. Key points - A BMI over 27.4 in women or over 29.4 in men is a recognised risk factor for coccydynia. - In people with a higher BMI, the pelvis tilts back less when sitting, so the coccyx meets the seat end-on and can be pushed backward (luxation) . - In very thin people, the pelvis tilts back a lot and there is little padding, so the coccyx lies almost flat and can bend too far forward (hypermobility) . - Rapid weight loss may also play a part, though this is based on clinical experience rather than strong studies. What happens when you sit When you sit down, your pelvis rolls backward. Your weight is meant to rest mainly on the two sitting bones (ischial tuberosities), with the coccyx taking a small share and bending slightly forward. How far the pelvis rolls, and how much soft padding lies under it, decides how much load reaches the coccyx and in which direction. Body type How the pelvis tilts What happens to the coccyx Typical finding Higher BMI Tilts back only a little Meets the seat almost end-on and is pushed backward Backward slip of a joint (posterior luxation) Healthy BMI Moderate tilt Bends forward slightly (5–25°) while the sitting bones take most of the weight Normal movement Low BMI or rapid weight loss Tilts back a lot; little padding Lies almost flat and is bent forward Excessive bending (hypermobility) How body weight changes the way the coccyx is loaded (after Maigne et al., 2000; Garg and Ahuja, 2021). In Maigne's study of 208 patients, obesity was confirmed as a risk factor, and the types of coccyx damage differed between obese, normal-weight and thin people. In women whose pain started after childbirth, a BMI above 27 was linked to a higher rate of luxation (Maigne 2012). What this means for you - If you are carrying extra weight , gradual weight loss can reduce the load on the coccyx. Lean slightly forward when sitting, and use a cut-out cushion so the tip doesn't meet the seat. - If you are very slim or have lost weight quickly , avoid hard seats, add padding, and take frequent breaks from sitting. - Either way , the right treatment depends on how your coccyx is moving. That is why we examine carefully before treating.

title: Sitting with tailbone pain: 8 practical ways to ease it
summary: Desk job, long drives or a hard classroom bench? Small changes to how and how long you sit can take a lot of pressure off a sore coccyx.
text: If your tailbone hurts, sitting is usually the hardest part of the day. When you sit upright or lean back, part of your weight rests on the coccyx, the small bone at the very bottom of the spine. When it is bruised, inflamed or moving abnormally, that pressure turns into pain, and getting up from a chair can bring a sharp jolt. The good news is that how you sit makes a real difference. These are the changes our patients find most useful. 1. Lean slightly forward Tilting your upper body a little forward shifts your weight onto your thigh bones and the "sitting bones" of your pelvis, and off the coccyx. Sitting on the front half of the chair with your feet flat on the floor makes this easier. 2. Use a cut-out cushion A wedge or U-shaped cushion with a gap at the back lets the tailbone hang free instead of pressing on the seat. Round "doughnut" rings help some people but can still press on the coccyx, so a cushion with an open back is usually better. Take it with you: to the office, the car and restaurants. 3. Choose firm seats over soft sofas It sounds backwards, but deep, soft sofas let you sink and roll back onto the tailbone. A firm, supportive chair with a cushion is kinder. 4. Get up every 30 minutes Pressure and stiffness build the longer you sit. Set a reminder to stand, walk a few steps or do a gentle stretch every half hour. On long drives, plan short breaks. 5. Stand up the smart way Shift forward to the edge of the seat, bring your feet back under you, and push up through your legs while keeping your back straight. This avoids rocking back onto the coccyx at the moment you rise. 6. Support your lower back A small cushion or rolled towel behind the lower back keeps you upright and stops you slumping, which tips weight back onto the tailbone. 7. Heat or ice For a few minutes at a time, a warm pack can relax tight muscles around the coccyx, and an ice pack wrapped in a cloth can calm a flare-up. Use whichever helps you more. 8. Keep your bowels comfortable Straining often makes tailbone pain worse. Plenty of water, fruit, vegetables and fibre help. If bowel movements are painful, ask your doctor or pharmacist about a gentle stool softener. When self-care isn't enough Most tailbone pain settles with time and sensible habits. If yours hasn't improved after a few weeks, keeps coming back, or stops you working or sleeping, it is worth having the coccyx and surrounding muscles properly examined. A displaced or stiff coccyx, or tight pelvic-floor muscles, often needs hands-on treatment rather than more waiting. See a doctor promptly if the pain comes with fever, numbness, leg weakness, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels.

title: Tailbone pain after pregnancy: why it happens and what helps
summary: Many new mothers find that sitting to feed their baby is surprisingly painful. Here is why childbirth can affect the coccyx, and how it is treated.
text: Tailbone pain is much more common in women than in men, and pregnancy and childbirth are among the main reasons. Many mothers notice it in the weeks after delivery, often while sitting to feed the baby, which is exactly when sitting is hardest to avoid. Why pregnancy and childbirth affect the coccyx - Hormones loosen the joints. During pregnancy, hormones relax the ligaments of the pelvis so the baby can pass through. The joint between the sacrum and the coccyx loosens too. - The baby's head presses on the coccyx during a vaginal delivery, pushing it backwards. Occasionally the coccyx is bruised, strained or even displaced. - Weight and posture change. Through pregnancy, the way you sit and stand changes, putting new strain on the lower spine and pelvic floor. - Assisted or long deliveries and larger babies make injury a little more likely. What it typically feels like - An ache or sharp pain right at the base of the spine - Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and when standing up - Sometimes painful bowel movements or discomfort during intercourse What helps 1. A cut-out (wedge or U-shaped) cushion for feeding and for the car. 2. Feeding positions that take weight off the tailbone: lying on your side, or sitting leaning slightly forward with good back support. 3. Gentle pelvic-floor exercises once your midwife or doctor says it is safe. 4. Keeping stools soft: fluids and fibre, and avoiding straining. 5. Heat or cold packs for short periods. Before taking pain relief while breastfeeding, check with your doctor or pharmacist which medicines are suitable. When to get it checked Postnatal tailbone pain often eases over a few weeks. If it lasts longer than that, keeps returning, or makes caring for your baby difficult, ask for an examination. When the coccyx has been pushed out of its normal position or the surrounding muscles stay in spasm, hands-on treatment can help a great deal, and you don't need to "just put up with it". See a doctor urgently if you have fever, a wound or swelling near the tailbone, numbness, or new problems with bladder or bowel control.

title: Tailbone pain red flags: when it needs urgent attention
summary: Most tailbone pain is mechanical and treatable without surgery. A few warning signs, though, mean you should see a doctor quickly. Here is what they are.
text: The vast majority of tailbone pain comes from a fall, childbirth, long sitting or strain on the coccyx and the muscles around it. It is uncomfortable and can be stubborn, but it isn't dangerous. Rarely, though, pain at the base of the spine is a sign of something that needs prompt medical care. See a doctor promptly if you have tailbone pain with: - Fever, chills or feeling generally unwell. This could mean an infection, such as an abscess or an infected cyst near the tailbone (a pilonidal cyst). - A lump, swelling, redness or a wound near the tailbone. - Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer. Very occasionally, a growth in or near the sacrum or coccyx causes pain. - Pain that is severe and getting steadily worse , or pain that is just as bad lying down at night. - Pain after a major accident such as a road traffic collision or a fall from height, where a fracture is possible. Go to an emergency department straight away if you have: - Numbness around the buttocks, genitals or inner thighs (sometimes called "saddle" numbness) - New difficulty passing urine, or loss of bladder or bowel control - Weakness in one or both legs These can be signs of pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal, which needs urgent assessment. Why a proper examination matters Because so many conditions can cause pain low in the back and pelvis, a specialist first takes a careful history and examines the coccyx, the joints around it and the pelvic muscles. When needed, X-rays taken sitting and standing can show whether the coccyx moves abnormally, and an MRI can rule out other causes. Only once the cause is clear should treatment begin. If none of the warning signs above apply, tailbone pain is usually treatable with self-care and targeted, hands-on therapy. Surgery is rarely needed.

title: What happens at a coccydynia consultation (and how to prepare)
summary: Nervous about your first visit for tailbone pain? Here is what to expect, step by step, and how to prepare so you get the most from the appointment.
text: Many people put off getting tailbone pain checked because they aren't sure what the visit involves, or they feel embarrassed. Knowing what happens makes it much easier. Before you come - Make a list of your medicines and any past operations or injuries. - Note how your pain behaves: when it started, what makes it worse (sitting, getting up, driving, bowel movements) and what helps. - Wear comfortable clothes. - If you would prefer to be seen by a female clinician , mention it when booking. 1. Listening and history The visit starts with a conversation: how the pain began (a fall, childbirth, long sitting or no clear reason), how long you have had it, how it affects your work, sleep and daily life, and what you have already tried. 2. Examination The clinician examines your lower back, pelvis and the area around the tailbone, checking for tenderness, swelling and how the coccyx and surrounding muscles respond to pressure and movement. Everything is explained first, and nothing happens without your consent. You can ask to pause at any time. 3. Pinpointing the cause The aim is to find out what is actually causing the pain: whether the coccyx is moving too much, too little or sitting out of position, whether the pelvic-floor muscles are in spasm, or whether something else needs ruling out. 4. Treatment plan You'll leave with a clear plan. Depending on the cause, this may include hands-on treatment such as manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles, together with posture and seating advice, a suitable cushion, and exercises you can do at home. Many patients notice a difference early, but the plan is always tailored to your own situation. 5. Follow-up After treatment, a short check-in a week or two later helps track your pain and sitting tolerance, so the plan can be adjusted if needed. title: Why Some Tailbone Pain Treatments Fail: The Importance of Functional Assessment
summary: Chronic tailbone pain can be frustrating because many patients visit multiple healthcare providers and undergo various treatments without lasting…
text: Chronic tailbone pain can be frustrating because many patients visit multiple healthcare providers and undergo various treatments without lasting improvement. This often happens when treatment focuses only on symptom management rather than identifying the root cause of the pain. Patients may receive medications, anti-inflammatory drugs, injections, or advice to use cushions. While these approaches can temporarily reduce discomfort, they may not address underlying biomechanical dysfunctions affecting the coccyx, pelvis, and surrounding muscles. As a result, pain frequently returns once the temporary effects of treatment wear off. Common Signs That the Underlying Cause Has Not Been Addressed Certain symptoms may indicate that the primary source of coccyx pain remains untreated: - Pain that returns shortly after medication is stopped - Persistent discomfort despite normal MRI or X-ray findings - Difficulty sitting for extended periods - Pain during transitions from sitting to standing - Recurring episodes of tailbone pain after temporary relief - Ongoing pelvic or lower back tightness Recognizing these warning signs can help patients seek a more comprehensive evaluation. The Relationship Between Posture and Tailbone Pain Posture plays a significant role in the development and persistence of coccyx pain. Poor sitting habits can place excessive pressure on the tailbone, especially during prolonged office work, driving, or sedentary lifestyles. Common postural factors include: - Slouched sitting posture - Leaning backward excessively while seated - Uneven weight distribution - Poor workstation ergonomics - Reduced core muscle support Over time, these habits can contribute to increased stress on the coccyx and surrounding structures. How Muscle Imbalances Contribute to Coccyx Pain The tailbone functions as part of a larger musculoskeletal system involving the pelvis, hips, lower back, and pelvic floor muscles. Tight or weak muscles in any of these areas can alter movement patterns and increase pressure on the coccyx. Some patients develop compensatory muscle tension due to previous injuries, prolonged sitting, pregnancy, or chronic pain conditions. Identifying and correcting these imbalances is often essential for long-term recovery. Benefits of Early Functional Assessment Seeking specialized assessment early can help prevent chronic pain from becoming more severe. A detailed functional evaluation can identify movement restrictions, postural abnormalities, muscle imbalances, and mechanical factors that may not be visible on imaging studies. Early intervention may help: - Reduce pain more effectively - Improve sitting tolerance - Restore normal movement patterns - Prevent recurrent flare-ups - Improve overall quality of life When to Seek Professional Help Patients should consider professional evaluation if tailbone pain: - Persists for more than a few weeks - Interferes with work or daily activities - Makes sitting difficult - Returns repeatedly despite treatment - Is associated with previous trauma or childbirth Early diagnosis and targeted rehabilitation often lead to better outcomes and faster recovery. Long-Term Recovery Strategy Addressing the root cause rather than simply masking symptoms improves long-term outcomes. Conclusion Many tailbone pain treatments fail because they focus only on pain relief. Comprehensive functional assessment and individualized rehabilitation provide a more effective solution. FAQs 1. Why do painkillers not provide permanent relief? They reduce symptoms but do not address underlying mechanical problems. 2. What is a functional assessment? It evaluates posture, movement patterns, muscle function, and biomechanics. 3. Can poor sitting habits worsen coccyx pain? Yes. Incorrect sitting mechanics can increase coccyx stress. 4. Is every tailbone pain case the same? No. Each patient may have different contributing factors. 5. What makes personalized rehabilitation effective? Treatment is tailored to the patient’s specific dysfunction and symptoms.

title: Tailbone Pain While Sitting: Understanding the Real Mechanical Cause

title: Bruised Tailbone: Requires Special Precautions. Slow to Heal
summary: A freak accident or injury may lead to Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone. The coccyx, another name for the tailbone is situated in a medically…
text: Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone A freak accident or injury may lead to Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone . The coccyx, another name for the tailbone is situated in a medically inaccessible place. It is located at the lowest portion of the back and comprises the last vertebral column of the spine. It is made up of 3 to 5 bony elements, which are held in place by ligaments and joints. An injured coccyx or Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone can take a long time to heal. Hence, it takes longer to heal and requires extra care. The majority of coccyx injuries occur in women since they have a broader pelvis. Common Causes of Coccyx Injury The most common ways to injure your tailbone are: - Falling down in a seated stance, which impacts the tailbone the most - Getting directly hit on the coccyx, for e.g. during sports - Childbirth can also injure or fracture the tailbone There are other, though less common causes of Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone injury like nerve root compression, bone spurs, injury to another part of the spine, local infections or even tumours. Sometimes, you may feel pain in the tailbone area without realizing it has been injured. However, you can still determine exactly where the damage occurred. Symptoms of Coccyx Damage Pain is the overwhelming symptom of an injured tailbone. The pain can be in different areas like: - Pain or numbness while sitting down - Tenderness or pain in the lower back - Swelling or bruising at the base of the spinal cord - Pain near the top of the buttocks - Pain in bed while rolling over - Pain while in the latrine - In severe case the pain or numbness can shoot down the backs of the legs Medical Intervention When the tailbone is damaged due to any cause, the pain will immediately compel you to see your Doctor. The first thing the physician will recommend is an X-ray to confirm if there is a Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone . The first sign of a broken tailbone is pain when direct pressure is applied to it. Other reasons why immediate medical attention may be called for include: - Pain, numbness or tingling in the tailbone area - Swelling or pain in the tailbone region - If the pain has been ignored but persists - Weakness or shooting pain in the legs - Persistent Constipation - Issues with controlling bowel or bladder movements If you’re experiencing sudden pain in your tailbone region only trained medical professional can tell you if the strong discomfort is related to the tailbone trauma or to a more serious disease. A coccyx injury rarely requires emergency room attention, but timely medical intervention can give you the specialized care and treatment that a damaged coccyx or Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone demands. Healing an Injured Coccyx It takes a considerable amount of time to treat an injured coccyx or Bruised Tailbone Fractured Tailbone , but even that depends on the severity of the damage. A fractured tailbone takes anywhere between 8 and 12 weeks to heal. If the coccyx is only bruised, it can still take about 4 weeks to heal completely. If the pain and discomfort is not responding to treatment you may need steroid injections or even surgery to remove a portion of the coccyx. However, the last option may not be considered until 6 months post injury. Can You Speed up Recovery? The patient needs to understand that whatever he or she does, it should not worsen the condition. He or she should consult a doctor, take it easy and give the area the chance to heal. It is important not to undertake any physical activity, which causes discomfort or pain. Resting is key to the healing process and the time it takes. Do not take pain killers for the first 24 hours post injury, since the medicine tends to increase the chances of bleeding. Take pain medication as when required after 24 hours. If you have heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney or liver disease, have had stomach ulcers or internal bleeding at any time, confirm with the doctor that the prescribed medications will cause no further complications It can be very painful when rolling over to get out of bed in the mornings. The technique is to move slowly and to get out of bed by pulling oneself into a fetal posture. Then swing your legs out in front but step to the ground slowly. Avoid sitting on hard surfaces but do not sit for long periods of time even on soft ones. Make it a habit of sitting on cushions. You will need to purchase a gel donut or a cushion prescribed by the doctor. Apply ice to the tailbone area for 20 minutes per hour for the first 48 hours post injury. However, do not apply the ice directly to the skin. After 48 hours of the injury, the patient must switch to heat pads, but should not heat for more than 20 minutes per application.

text: Lets understand the basic of Coccydynia and causes of Coccydynia during pregnancy. Tailbone pain is the most common aches that pregnant women experience through out Pregnancy. What is Coccydynia/ Tailbone Pain? Pain in or around the coccyx at the bottom of spine is termed as Coccydynia. What are the Causes for Coccyx Pain During Pregnancy? Pregnancy hormones plays a vital role. During pregnancy, our body makes hormone called as Relaxing together with Estrogen causes joints and ligaments on pelvic floor to relax & stretch, allowing the coccyx to shift more than usual. As pregnancy progress, the growing baby’s start pressing over coccyx which increases the pressure on coccyx bone leading to discomfort and pain in coccyx. How to Relieve Coccydynia? Things to be done to relieve the pain are: Meet a Specialist for Coccydynia in India for advice’s and measure’s to be taken to avoid further injury www.Tailbonetreatment.com a) Applying warm or cold packs over coccyx area twice a day. b) Avoid long sitting and long travels. c) Use Tailbone Treatment Cushion to sit (Click here to buy a certified Tailbone Treatment Cushion). d) Frequently change positions. e) Gentle stretches for the spine to increase mobility and relieve pressure off the tailbone under specialist guidance. f) Postural correction through out pregnancy. title: Post Pregnancy Low Back Pain Could be Recti Divarication (Abdominal Splitting)
summary: Diastasis Recti/Recti Divarication/Abdominal splitting is a midline separation of muscles of the abdominal wall. A palpable midline gap of more than 2 cm or…
text: Diastasis Recti/Recti Divarication/Abdominal splitting is a midline separation of muscles of the abdominal wall. A palpable midline gap of more than 2 cm or any visible bulging on exertion is considered as Recti Divarication . This separation is a normal occurrence of pregnancy, which is only a problem if the muscles do not go back to their correct position. How does it happen? Diastasis Recti Abdominis commonly occurs around the umbilicus. It is a result of abdominal musculature stretch weakness from maternal hormonal changes and increased tension by the growing uterus. Diastasis Recti can occur in varying degrees during pregnancy and may not resolve spontaneously in the postpartum period. Why treatment of Recti Divarication is necessary? Diastasis Recti (Abdominal Splitting) is commonly seen in women who have multiple pregnancies, which will make the muscles weaker. This separation & weaker abdominal muscle can cause an array of problems, contribute to - Back pain, - Coccydynia/Tailbone Pain, - Bad posture, - Pelvic floor dysfunctions, - Urinary Incontinence (Uncontrolled urination) - Hernia, - Cosmetic defects. Back and/or pelvic pains are the most common manifestation of a Diastasis Recti Abdominis. A retrospective study done in 2007 by Spitznagle et al found that 66% of all patients with Diastasis Recti had support-related pelvic floor dysfunction (SPFD) diagnosis of stress urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapsed. How to diagnose this condition? Ultrasonography (real-time ultrasound imaging) is an accurate method to measure rectus diastasis above the umbilicus and at the umbilical level. A small separation of the midline at the abdominals, approximately one to two fingers’ width, is common after most pregnancies, and is not a problem. But if the gap at the midline is: • More than 2 1/2 finger widths • Does not shrink as the patient tighten her abdominals or • A small Protrusion at her midline of abdomen then she probably have Diastasis Recti Abdominis and need to take a few special precautions during exercise and other activities. What is the treatment for Diastasis Recti Dysfunction? Conservative management, such as specific therapeutic exercises directed by a physiotherapist, or health care professional well-acquainted with Diastasis Recti.Such exercises are aimed at strengthening the deep core muscles, such as the transverses abdominis and pelvic floor muscles. Poorly executed abdominal exercises can cause an increase in intra-abdominal pressure, this force may cause further recti separation and its accompanying bulge/hernia to worsen. Hence, it is important to monitor Diastasis Recti Abdominis (and the hernia if any) before prescribing any abdominal exercises. Unsuitable abdominal exercises include sit ups, straight leg raises, Pilates movements i.e. “the 100s” and especially trunk rotation activities, such as criss-cross sit ups which target the obliques, can strain the abdominals excessively. What are the level of prognosis? The patient usually does very well. In most cases, recti diastasis usually heals on its own over a postpartum period of 6 weeks to 3 months. However, Diastasis Recti Abdominis may also persist long after the woman delivered. Further intervention may be required if recovery of Diastasis Recti Abdominis does not occur. Specific therapeutic exercise may help improve the condition. Umbilical hernia may occur in some cases. If pain is present, surgery may be needed. In general, complications only result when a hernia develops.
